title: Puzzles to learn python loops
summary:
Problem : 1
Divide the Tiles Equally
A school is preparing a large square floor for its annual function. The floor has N tiles arranged in a single row. The teacher wants to divide these tiles into equal-sized groups without leaving any tile unused. For example, if there are 12 tiles, the teacher can make:

1 group of 12 tiles
2 groups of 6 tiles
3 groups of 4 tiles
4 groups of 3 tiles
6 groups of 2 tiles
12 groups of 1 tile

no = 12
divisor = 1
while divisor <= 12:
    if no % divisor == 0:
        print(divisor)
    divisor = divisor + 1

Problem : 2
The Special Lock Number

A treasure box has a number lock with a number N. The lock designer follows a special rule: A number is considered a Special Number if it can be divided equally into groups in only two ways:
One group containing all the items.
Groups containing one item each.
For example, if the number is 7, the items can be arranged equally only as:
1 group of 7 or 7 groups of 1. But if the number is 8, it can also be arranged as 2 groups of 4, so it is not a Special Number.

Write a Python program that accepts a number N and determines whether it is a Special Number or not.

N = int(input("Enter a number: "))

divisor = 1
count = 0

while divisor <= N:
    if N % divisor == 0:
        count = count + 1
    divisor = divisor + 1

if count == 2:
    print("Special Number")
else:
    print("Not a Special Number")

Problem : 3
Secret VIP Numbers

A security system assigns special numbers to the first few VIP lockers. A number is considered a VIP number if it can be divided exactly by only 1 and itself. The security officer wants the numbers of the first 5 VIP lockers. Write a Python program to display those 5 numbers.

num = 2
count = 0

while count < 5:
    divisor = 1
    factors = 0

    while divisor <= num:
        if num % divisor == 0:
            factors = factors + 1
        divisor = divisor + 1

    if factors == 2:
        print(num)     // 2 3 5 7 11
        count = count + 1

    num = num + 1

Problem : 4
16.2) The Special Numbers
A teacher is preparing a Number Exhibition for students. She writes the numbers 1 to 20 on 20 cards. She wants to select only the special cards. A card is special if its number can be divided exactly by only two numbers: 1 and the number itself.

The teacher asks the students:
“Check all the cards from 1 to 20 and display the numbers that are special.”

num = 1

while num <= 20:
    divisor = 1
    count = 0

    while divisor <= num:
        if num % divisor == 0:
            count = count + 1
        divisor = divisor + 1

    if count == 2:
        print(num)  //2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19
    num = num + 1

title: How to Turn Speech into Text on a Computer
summary:
Typing a long text by hand is slow. We can speak faster than we type, so it is handy when the computer turns your speech into text by itself. Below is how to turn speech into text on a computer, and which way is simpler.

Why you might need it

  • Quickly write an email, a note or a message without typing.

  • Capture a thought before it slips away.

  • Turn a voice note into text.

  • Write when your hands are busy or tired.

Way 1. The built-in Windows voice typing

Windows has voice typing built in: press Win + H in any text field and speak. It is free and needs no installation. The downsides: it needs the internet, the settings are scattered around the system, and you often have to fix punctuation by hand.

Way 2. Online services

There are websites where you can speak into the microphone or upload a recording and get text back. Handy for a one-off task, but keep in mind: your voice goes to someone else's server. For personal or work recordings that is not always a good idea.

Way 3. A simple program on your computer

If you want it simple, with no fuss over settings, a dedicated program fits well. VoiceNote is made for exactly that: press “Record” and speak — the app types your speech as text for you. You can copy or save the finished text. The interface is simple: one Record button, one Stop button.

More about the VoiceNote program

How to dictate for cleaner text

  • Speak evenly and not too fast.

  • Make short pauses between phrases.

  • Record in a quiet place, with no background noise.

  • Check the finished text and fix the punctuation.

FAQ

Do I need an expensive microphone?**No. A regular laptop or headset microphone is fine — the main thing is to speak clearly.

Which language does it work in?****Russian and other languages.

Will my speech go to someone else's server?**
VoiceNote runs on your own computer and does not send texts outside.

In short

  • Fast and free — the built-in Windows voice typing (Win + H).

  • A one-off, non-personal task — online is fine.

  • Simple and on your own computer — VoiceNote: press Record, speak, get text.

Originally published at evgeniymamonov.com.

title: How to get transcripts from an entire YouTube playlist (no API key)
summary:
Disclosure: I made the Actor used in this article, so I'm biased. Apify links here are referral links. The same steps work with any tool that gives you captions; I note the free alternative below.

You have a YouTube playlist, say a 40-video course, and you want the text of every video. Maybe it's for a ChatGPT or Claude knowledge base, for notes, or to search across a whole series. Copy-pasting 40 transcripts by hand is a bad afternoon.

Here is how to get all of them in one go, with Python, and without a YouTube Data API key or a Google Cloud project. The result is a CSV and one Markdown file you can drop into an AI tool.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.9 or newer
  • A free Apify account (new accounts include free monthly platform credit, so the example below costs well under a cent; please check the current credit on Apify's pricing page)
  • Your Apify API token, from Settings → API & Integrations 
pip install -U apify-client pandas
export APIFY_TOKEN="your-token-here"

Step 1: Run the Actor on your playlist

YouTube Transcript & Subtitles Scraper takes playlist, channel or video links and returns one row per video. Pricing is $0.004 per transcript delivered ($4 per 1,000). Videos with no captions are not charged.

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("logicbase_systems/youtube-transcript").call(run_input={
    "playlistUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDNU6R1_67000Dx_ZCJB-3pi"],
    "maxVideosPerSource": 3,   # raise this for the whole playlist
    "languages": ["en"],
    "includeSegments": False,  # plain text only, smaller output
})

I used a short public playlist (3Blue1Brown's neural networks series) and maxVideosPerSource: 3 so you can test cheaply. Change the number, or leave it at the default of 20, once you're happy.

Step 2: Read the results 

rows = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
ok = [r for r in rows if r["status"] == "ok"]
print(f"{len(ok)} transcripts, {len(rows) - len(ok)} videos without a transcript")

Every row has status. Videos that have no captions come back as status: "error" with a reason such as NO_CAPTIONS, so one bad video never breaks the whole run. Each good row has the title, channel, publish date, word count, language, and the full text.

When I ran exactly this code, I got 3 transcripts back in a few seconds.

Step 3: Save as CSV and as one file for AI tools 

df = pd.DataFrame(ok)[["title", "channelName", "publishDate", "wordCount", "text", "videoUrl"]]
df.to_csv("playlist_transcripts.csv", index=False)

with open("playlist_transcripts.md", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for r in ok:
        f.write(f"# {r['title']}\n{r['videoUrl']}\n\n{r['text']}\n\n")

You now have a spreadsheet-friendly CSV and a single Markdown file with a heading and link per video. Upload the Markdown file to ChatGPT, Claude or NotebookLM, or split it into chunks for a RAG pipeline.

Useful options

Option What it does
languages: ["en", "hi"] Preferred languages, in order. Human-made captions are used first, automatic ones as a fallback.
includeSrt: true Adds the transcript as SRT subtitle text.
includeSegments: true Adds timestamped caption lines (start, duration, text).
channelUrls Same thing for a whole channel: it takes the newest videos first.
videoUrls A plain list of video links, mixed freely with playlists and channels.

Things to know before you rely on it

  • It reads captions that already exist on the video, human-made or YouTube's automatic ones. It does not listen to audio, so videos with captions turned off can't be transcribed.
  • Automatic captions can contain mistakes, especially with names and technical terms.
  • Check that your use of the text respects YouTube's terms and the video owners' copyright.

The free DIY alternative

If you only have a few videos and don't mind some setup, you can do it yourself with yt-dlp:

yt-dlp --skip-download --write-subs --write-auto-subs --sub-langs "en.*" --convert-subs srt "PLAYLIST_URL"

That works well from your own computer. The catch is that YouTube often blocks or rate-limits requests that come from cloud servers, so a script that runs fine locally can fail once you deploy it. Handling that (rotating IPs, retries) is the part a hosted tool takes off your hands.

Next steps

  • Run the same code on a channel: replace playlistUrls with "channelUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/@3blue1brown"].
  • Schedule it on Apify to pull each new video's transcript automatically.
  • Send the output to Google Sheets, Notion or a vector database with Apify's n8n, Make or Zapier integrations.
  • Ready-made versions: playlist to transcripts, channel transcripts, subtitles to SRT, plain text for AI.

If something doesn't work for you, open an issue on the Actor page and I'll look at it.

title: Finding two ClickHouse time zone bugs with a differential test
summary:
I wanted a cheap way to find real bugs in a large database, so I stopped reading code and compared answers instead. Two of the comparisons found genuine bugs in ClickHouse's date functions, both in time zones with a UTC offset that is not a whole number of hours. The other three comparisons found nothing, which is also worth knowing.

Both fixes are open pull requests, not merged. I say so up front because the title of a post like this tends to promise more than the state of the work.

The method: ask the same question two ways

A differential test needs no expected values. You run the same logical query through two routes that must agree, and print any disagreement:

  • Against a reference. ClickHouse's date functions against Python's zoneinfo.
  • Against itself. The same JOIN with every join algorithm. The same filter with the primary key, skip indexes and PREWHERE on and off. The same GROUP BY with two-level, external and in-order aggregation.

Each probe is about 40-70 lines of Python that shells out to clickhouse local. They are public gists, with the setup in the header: date functions, JOIN algorithms, index analysis, aggregation settings.

Bug 1: toStartOfHour returns :30 on a day when the clocks move by 30 minutes

Australia/Lord_Howe shifts by 30 minutes twice a year. The probe compares toStartOfHour over thousands of timestamps with what Python says the wall clock hour is. Only two samples out of 4,000 disagreed, both on a transition day:

SELECT toStartOfHour(toDateTime('2024-04-07 03:10:00', 'Australia/Lord_Howe'));
-- 2024-04-07 02:30:00   (expected 03:00:00)

Every other sample, including all the other days of the year in that zone, was right. The test only found this because it sampled around transitions on purpose. The cause is that toStartOfHour ends in a function that rounds on a grid anchored at the local midnight. After a 30 minute shift, that grid no longer lines up with the clock. toStartOfInterval(..., INTERVAL 2 HOUR) already compensated for the shift, so the 2-hour answer was right and the 1-hour answer wrong for the same input.

The fix applies the same compensation to the 1-hour case, only when the day's shift is not a whole number of hours.

Two things I learned from the CI run:

  1. I could not build ClickHouse here, so CI was the first time the test ran. It passed.
  2. The performance comparison, which is part of the CI, flagged date_time_long at +51.7% on my first push. I had added a second lookup of the day to the hot path. Looking the day up once removed it. A correct fix can still be a regression, and the benchmark caught it before a reviewer had to.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131620.

Bug 2: minute intervals before 1970 round to the wrong boundary 

SET enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1;
SELECT toStartOfFifteenMinutes(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'));          -- 12:00:00
SELECT toStartOfInterval(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE);  -- 11:54:00

toStartOfInterval has an arithmetic shortcut that rounds the Unix timestamp. Before 1970 it was allowed whenever the offsets were whole minutes. The dedicated functions round from the local midnight there. The two agree only if the offset is a multiple of the interval, and Warsaw was at +01:24 until 1915. Checking the neighbours turned up Pacific/Chatham (+12:45), where even INTERVAL 10 MINUTE was wrong in 1960.

The fix narrows the condition: whole hours that divide into the interval. Other zones take the slower generic path before the epoch, which is what the dedicated functions use.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131915.

What found nothing

  • JOIN algorithms (hash, parallel_hash, grace_hash, full_sorting_merge, partial_merge, direct, auto) over NULL, NaN, tuple, array, map, LowCardinality and decimal keys: no disagreement over 7 random seeds.
  • Index analysis (primary key, three skip index types, PREWHERE, the old analyzer, the query condition cache) against a full scan over 14 key types: about 6,000 comparisons, no disagreement.
  • Aggregation settings against GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ROLLUP, window functions on composite keys: about 3,200 comparisons, no disagreement.

That is a useful result about the database. It is also a reminder that most of a mature system is correct, and the bugs live in the corners where two correct-looking pieces of logic meet, here "round to the hour" and "the offset changed by 30 minutes today".

The probes lied to me first

Most of my debugging time went on the harness, not on ClickHouse:

  • A first run reported thousands of mismatches. DateTime is unsigned, so negative timestamps clamp to 1970, and my Python side disagreed with that. I limited the range.
  • toStartOfMonth returns a Date, which has no time zone, so comparing its Unix timestamp with Python's local midnight is meaningless. I compared dates instead.
  • -0.0 and 0.0 group together but print differently, so the probe flagged a representative choice as a bug. I removed -0.0 from the value pool.
  • clickhouse local keeps tables between runs, and running several seeds in parallel locked its directory. I gave each run its own path and a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS.

If your first differential test reports a flood of bugs, it is almost always the test.

Takeaways

  • A reference implementation in another language is a good oracle for date and time code, because the two have different bugs.
  • Sample around the edges on purpose. The Lord Howe bug showed up in 2 of 4,000 timestamps.
  • When a fix touches a hot path, read the performance results, not only the tests.
  • Say whether your fix is merged. Mine are not, yet.

title: I make 60-second CS explainer videos with no video editor: one HTML file, headless Chrome and ffmpeg
summary:
I run csip12.in, a small free study site for CBSE Class 11 and 12 Computer Science students in India. Students asked for short videos, so this month I started making 60-second explainers for topics like circuit switching and packet switching.

I do not own a video editor and I did not want to learn one. Instead, each video is a web page that knows how to draw any moment of itself, and a script that takes 30 photos of it per second. Here is how it works and what went wrong along the way.

1. The video is a pure function of time

The whole video is one HTML file at 1080×1920. It has a fixed layout (title, a speech-bubble caption, an SVG area for the animation, progress dots) and one important function:

function render(t) {
  let k = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < DUR.length; i++) if (t >= START[i]) k = i;  // which scene
  const lt = t - START[k];                                          // time inside it
  art.innerHTML = SCENES[k](lt, DUR[k]);                            // SVG string
  cap.innerHTML = CAPTIONS[k];
}

Each scene is a function (localTime, duration) => svgString. There is no requestAnimationFrame, no CSS transitions, no state carried from one frame to the next. Every frame is computed from t alone.

That one rule is what makes the rest easy. I can jump to second 37.4 and see exactly what that frame will look like. I can render frames out of order, or render one still per scene to check the layout before spending ten minutes on a full capture.

The animations are just small helpers on top of that:

const clamp = (x, a = 0, b = 1) => Math.min(b, Math.max(a, x));
const ease  = x => x < .5 ? 2*x*x : 1 - (-2*x + 2)**2 / 2;
// pop(lt, at): 0 before `at`, then a quick overshoot up to 1

A packet moving from router R1 to R2 is lerp(x1, x2, ease(clamp((lt - 1.2) / 0.8))). A label appearing at 2.5 s is scale = pop(lt, 2.5). Once you have five or six of these, building a scene goes surprisingly fast.

2. Taking the photos

A Python script starts Chrome headless with --remote-debugging-port, opens the page over the DevTools protocol, and then loops:

for i in range(int(TOTAL * FPS)):
    await call('Runtime.evaluate', expression=f'render({i / FPS})')
    shot = await call('Page.captureScreenshot', format='jpeg', quality=92)
    save(f'frames/f{i:05d}.jpg', shot['data'])

Two details mattered:

  • Fonts. Before the first frame, I wait on document.fonts.ready and print which font families actually loaded. A fallback font in frame 1 and the real font in frame 40 looks like a glitch.
  • Window size. Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride with 1080×1920 and deviceScaleFactor: 1, so the screenshot is exactly one video frame with no scaling.

A 60-second video is 1,800 screenshots. On my laptop that takes a few minutes, which is fine.

3. Timing comes from the voice, not the other way round

I write the narration first, one line per scene, and generate each line with a text-to-speech model running locally. Then the build script:

  1. trims the silence at both ends of every line with ffmpeg's silenceremove (run forwards, reversed, and forwards again so it trims the end too),
  2. measures each trimmed clip with ffprobe,
  3. sets each scene's duration to the line's length plus 0.85 s of breathing room,
  4. writes those durations into a copy of the HTML file before capturing.

So if I rewrite a sentence and it gets longer, the scene simply gets longer. Nothing needs to be re-timed by hand.

The audio is one ffmpeg -filter_complex: each voice line is delayed to its scene start with adelay, everything is mixed with amix, a quiet background track is added at 8% volume, and loudnorm=I=-14 brings the result to the loudness that YouTube and Facebook expect. The background music is also generated, a four-chord loop of sine waves written with NumPy, so there is nothing to license.

4. Things that bit me

Stale frames. I once shortened a video and the output came out longer than before. The capture had written frames 0–1,850 into a folder that still held frames up to 1,950 from the previous, longer render, and ffmpeg's f%05d.jpg input happily used all of them. The build now deletes the frames folder before every capture.

Checking audio quality without listening to all of it. Local TTS on a 4 GB GPU sometimes returns a take that is just a hum or hiss. Instead of listening to every take, I render a tiny spectrogram for each line (showspectrumpic, 0–4 kHz). Real speech shows clear stacked harmonic stripes, and a bad take shows flat horizontal bars or uniform noise. I glance at ten small images and re-generate only the bad lines.

ffmpeg crashing on contact sheets. I wanted a grid of one still per scene to review layouts at a glance. hstack/xstack with a dozen inputs crashed ffmpeg on Windows with a heap error, so I tile the stills with Pillow instead. It is five lines of code and has never failed.

Text overflow. SVG text does not wrap and does not complain. A table cell like "Store & forward" at font size 38 quietly ran over its box. The only reliable check was the contact sheet: render the stills and look.

Why not just use a video editor?

For one video, an editor is faster. For a series, this approach wins: every video shares the same layout and helpers, so a new topic means writing about ten scene functions and ten sentences. Changing the brand colour or the caption font across all videos is a single line of CSS. And because the video lives in plain text files, I can keep old versions and see exactly what changed between them.

The first one, on circuit switching, is here: Circuit Switching in 60 seconds. The notes it is based on are on csip12.in, and I would be glad to hear from anyone who has built something similar, especially about speeding up the capture loop.

title: How I Built a 280-Page Kitchen Converter Site With a Python Static Generator and Cloudflare Pages
summary:
I recently built GramsInCup, a free grams-to-cups converter for home bakers. It looks like a simple calculator, but getting the numbers right and keeping ~280 pages fast and cheap to host turned into a fun little engineering project. Here is how it works.

The problem: one number doesn't fit all ingredients

Most quick converters treat a cup as a fixed weight. That breaks baking, because a cup is a volume:

  • 1 cup of all-purpose flour ≈ 125 g
  • 1 cup of granulated sugar ≈ 200 g
  • 1 cup of honey ≈ 340 g

So the core data is a list of ingredients, each with its own grams-per-cup value (based on the US cup, 236.588 ml):

INGREDIENTS = [
    # key, name, category, grams per US cup
    ("all-purpose-flour", "All-purpose flour", "Flours & starches", 125),
    ("granulated-sugar", "Granulated sugar", "Sugars & sweeteners", 200),
    ("butter", "Butter", "Fats & oils", 226.8),
    ("honey", "Honey", "Sugars & sweeteners", 340),
    # ... 48 ingredients in total
]

Everything else (tablespoons, teaspoons, ml, ounces) is derived from that one value.

No framework, just a Python build script

The whole site is generated by a few plain Python files:

  • data.py: ingredient densities and unit definitions
  • build.py: renders the main tool pages, the shared header and footer, the sitemap and robots.txt
  • programmatic.py: generates one page per ingredient (for example "flour grams to cups")
  • blog.py: turns Markdown posts into HTML

There is no React, no bundler and no database. Each page is a string of HTML written to a dist folder. A full build takes a couple of seconds, and every page ships one small CSS file and one small JS file.

The converter itself is a short vanilla JS file. The build script injects the ingredient list into it as JSON, so the browser and the server-rendered tables always use the same data.

The rounding bug I didn't expect

The server-rendered tables (Python) and the live converter (JavaScript) disagreed on some values. The cause: Python's round() uses banker's rounding, so round(62.5) gives 62, while my JS used normal half-up rounding and showed 63.

The fix was a tiny helper so both sides round the same way:

import math

def rhu(x, nd=0):
    """round half up, like JavaScript Math.round"""
    m = 10 ** nd
    return math.floor(x * m + 0.5) / m

I also wrote a small Playwright script that loads every URL in the sitemap and checks that the numbers in the HTML match what the JS calculates. It catches this kind of drift before it goes live.

Showing cups the way people measure

Nobody measures "0.8 cups". The converter snaps results to kitchen fractions (⅛, ¼, ⅓, ⅜, ½, ⅝, ⅔, ¾, ⅞) and shows the exact decimal next to it, for example: 100 g of flour = ¾ cup (0.8 exactly).

Hosting: Cloudflare Pages, deployed from GitHub

The code lives in a GitHub repo. Cloudflare Pages runs the Python build on every push and serves the static output from its CDN. For a static site the free plan is plenty: unlimited bandwidth and 500 builds a month.

Blog posts are Markdown files edited through a Git-based CMS. Posts with a future date are skipped at build time, and a small GitHub Actions cron job makes an empty commit on the publish date, which triggers a rebuild and makes the post go live. That gives scheduled posts on a static site with no server.

An embeddable widget

I also made a tiny standalone converter page that other sites can embed with an iframe. It is a single HTML file with inline CSS and JS and no external requests, so it loads fast inside someone else's page.

What I'd do differently

  • Write the data-consistency test on day one instead of after the rounding bug.
  • Keep every number in one data file from the start. It made adding new ingredient pages trivial later.

If you're building a small tool site, a plain Python generator plus a free static host goes a surprisingly long way. Happy to answer questions about any part of the setup in the comments.

title: Ten Uniface forms without painting a single field - generating the XML instead
summary:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 had grown to more than a hundred services for sales: products, prices, quotes, orders, invoices, payments, dunning, deliveries, subscriptions, bank statements. None of it had a user interface yet. The next stage was ten new forms with between 11 and 58 fields each - 310 fields in total - plus one new button in the existing main menu.

Painting 310 fields one by one in the form painter is slow, and it is hard to keep a consistent layout. The IDE can export and import repository objects as XML, so the forms were generated as XML and imported instead. This article shows how that worked, what the form picture inside the XML looks like, and the one mistake that crashed the IDE.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. Paths are shortened to C:\Projects\CustomerApp\.

Start from a real export

The safest template is a form that already works. In the IDE, the menu at the top right (≡) has Export and Import XML.... Exporting one existing modal form gave a file with three tables:

Table Content
UFORM one occurrence: the form itself, with USCRIPT (the ProcScript), UDECLARATIONS (component variables), window size and FORMPIC
UXGROUP one occurrence per entity painted on the form
UXFIELD one occurrence per field: widget type, label, initial value, field script

The forms in this app all follow the same pattern: a non-database dummy entity (PRD_DMY.NOMODEL, DOC_DMY.NOMODEL, ...), labels as non-editable fields, single-line and multi-line edit boxes, and command buttons whose detail trigger calls an entry in the form script:

trigger detail
    call DO_SAVE
end

So the generator only needs four field kinds. It takes one field occurrence of each kind from the exported template and changes the name, the label, and for buttons the trigger script.

The form picture is text

The interesting part is FORMPIC. It is not binary; it is a text picture of the form, one line per row, and every painted object is a token. The entity token looks like this:

&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=PRD_DMY.NOMODEL&uSEP;WID=96&uSEP;HEI=32&uSEP;HOC=96&uSEP;VOC=32&uFRM;

and a field token like this:

&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_SAVE&uSEP;WID=16&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;

The position of a token is its column in the line. WID and HEI are the size in characters and rows. In the template, line 0 was empty, line 1 started with six spaces and the entity token, and the fields followed in the lines below.

The generator builds that picture from a list of rows. This is the code that was used for all ten forms (Python):

def token_e(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uSEP;HOC=%d&uSEP;VOC=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei, wid, hei)
def token_f(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei)
def formpic(ent, ewid, ehei, fields):
    rows = {}
    for f in fields:
        rows.setdefault(f['row'], []).append(f)
    lines = ['', '      ' + token_e(ent + '.NOMODEL', ewid, ehei)]
    maxrow = max(f['row'] + f['h'] - 1 for f in fields)
    for r in range(1, maxrow + 1):
        line = ''
        cur = 0
        for f in sorted(rows.get(r, []), key=lambda x: x['col']):
            c = f['col'] + 6
            assert c >= cur, (f['name'], c, cur)
            line += ' ' * (c - cur) + token_f(f['name'], f['w'], f['h'])
            cur = c + f['w']
        lines.append(line)

(The function ends by joining the lines with line breaks; the XML writer escapes & and writes the file as UTF-8 with BOM and CRLF, like the export.)

A layout is then just a list. This is the first block of the product form:

build('PRODUCT_FRM', 'PRD_DMY', [
 (1, [('LBL_SEARCH', L, 14), ('SEARCH', E, 30), ('BTN_SEARCH', B, 12), ('BTN_SEARCH_ALL', B, 24)]),
 (2, [('RESULT', M, 92, 8)]),
 ...

The + 6 that crashed the IDE

The first version did not have + 6. It placed the first field of each row at column 2 - which looked right, because in the painter the fields start just inside the entity frame.

The import reported success. Opening the form in the IDE did not:

Unhandled Exception
Error code  -100000   Description  Coding error
ERROR -10104    Internal error
COMPONENT UC_CPT   PROCNAME 109\GETPAINT   PROCLINE interrupt 22, FORMPIC.UFORM

The details pointed straight at FORMPIC. Comparing the generated picture with the template showed the difference: the entity token starts at column 6, and in the template the fields start at column 8. Column 2 put every field to the left of its own entity frame. The IDE does not validate that on import; it fails later, when it paints the form.

The dialog offers Exit and Ignore. Exit plus a restart of the IDE was the clean way out. After the fix (field columns relative to the entity, + 6), the corrected XML was imported over the broken form and opened normally.

Two lessons from this:

  • An import that succeeds is not a form that works. Always open and compile the imported object straight away.
  • Check the generator against a real export, not against your idea of the format.

A round-trip test for the generator

The second lesson became a test. A small parser reads the FORMPIC of the exported template back into a field list (name, row, column, width, height). Feeding that list into formpic() must give the original picture back, character for character. After the column fix, the round trip for the template form was identical. If the generator ever drifts from what the IDE writes, this test notices before the IDE does.

What else needed care

  • Button labels. The template's buttons all had the initial value "Button text". The forms set their labels in an entry SET_LABELS called from exec, so the XML did not need a label per button.
  • Default field triggers. Edit fields in the template carried a default onEdit trigger script. The generator drops it; the forms don't need it.
  • The import dialog. It sometimes closed itself after an import and sometimes stayed open. Typing the next file name without checking the dialog first sent the text into whatever had focus - once the open script editor. Check the dialog before typing.
  • Compile every form after import. Each of the ten forms (and the changed main menu) compiled with 0 errors and one warning: 1016, the dummy entity is not in the application model. That warning is expected for non-database entities.

Result

Ten forms, 310 fields, all generated from layout lists and the ProcScript source files. When a form needed a change - a label, a new button, a bug fix in the script - the source file changed, the XML was generated again and imported over the old form. After every import, the script in the repository was compared with the source file; all of them were identical.

The XML route does not replace the painter for a form that needs careful visual design. For many similar forms with a fixed pattern, it turned a lot of clicking into a list per form, and it made the layout reviewable as text.

The interesting part is FORMPIC. It is not binary; it is a text picture of the form, one line per row, and every painted object is a token. The entity token looks like this:

&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=PRD_DMY.NOMODEL&uSEP;WID=96&uSEP;HEI=32&uSEP;HOC=96&uSEP;VOC=32&uFRM;

and a field token like this:

&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_SAVE&uSEP;WID=16&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;

The position of a token is its column in the line. WID and HEI are the size in characters and rows. In the template, line 0 was empty, line 1 started with six spaces and the entity token, and the fields followed in the lines below.

The generator builds that picture from a list of rows. This is the code that was used for all ten forms (Python):

def token_e(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uSEP;HOC=%d&uSEP;VOC=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei, wid, hei)
def token_f(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei)
def formpic(ent, ewid, ehei, fields):
    rows = {}
    for f in fields:
        rows.setdefault(f['row'], []).append(f)
    lines = ['', '      ' + token_e(ent + '.NOMODEL', ewid, ehei)]
    maxrow = max(f['row'] + f['h'] - 1 for f in fields)
    for r in range(1, maxrow + 1):
        line = ''
        cur = 0
        for f in sorted(rows.get(r, []), key=lambda x: x['col']):
            c = f['col'] + 6
            assert c >= cur, (f['name'], c, cur)
            line += ' ' * (c - cur) + token_f(f['name'], f['w'], f['h'])
            cur = c + f['w']
        lines.append(line)

(The function ends by joining the lines with line breaks; the XML writer escapes & and writes the file as UTF-8 with BOM and CRLF, like the export.)

A layout is then just a list. This is the first block of the product form:

build('PRODUCT_FRM', 'PRD_DMY', [
 (1, [('LBL_SEARCH', L, 14), ('SEARCH', E, 30), ('BTN_SEARCH', B, 12), ('BTN_SEARCH_ALL', B, 24)]),
 (2, [('RESULT', M, 92, 8)]),
 ...

The + 6 that crashed the IDE

The first version did not have + 6. It placed the first field of each row at column 2 - which looked right, because in the painter the fields start just inside the entity frame.

The import reported success. Opening the form in the IDE did not:

Unhandled Exception
Error code  -100000   Description  Coding error
ERROR -10104    Internal error
COMPONENT UC_CPT   PROCNAME 109\GETPAINT   PROCLINE interrupt 22, FORMPIC.UFORM

The details pointed straight at FORMPIC. Comparing the generated picture with the template showed the difference: the entity token starts at column 6, and in the template the fields start at column 8. Column 2 put every field to the left of its own entity frame. The IDE does not validate that on import; it fails later, when it paints the form.

The dialog offers Exit and Ignore. Exit plus a restart of the IDE was the clean way out. After the fix (field columns relative to the entity, + 6), the corrected XML was imported over the broken form and opened normally.

Two lessons from this:

  • An import that succeeds is not a form that works. Always open and compile the imported object straight away.
  • Check the generator against a real export, not against your idea of the format.

A round-trip test for the generator

The second lesson became a test. A small parser reads the FORMPIC of the exported template back into a field list (name, row, column, width, height). Feeding that list into formpic() must give the original picture back, character for character. After the column fix, the round trip for the template form was identical. If the generator ever drifts from what the IDE writes, this test notices before the IDE does.

What else needed care

  • Button labels. The template's buttons all had the initial value "Button text". The forms set their labels in an entry SET_LABELS called from exec, so the XML did not need a label per button.
  • Default field triggers. Edit fields in the template carried a default onEdit trigger script. The generator drops it; the forms don't need it.
  • The import dialog. It sometimes closed itself after an import and sometimes stayed open. Typing the next file name without checking the dialog first sent the text into whatever had focus - once the open script editor. Check the dialog before typing.
  • Compile every form after import. Each of the ten forms (and the changed main menu) compiled with 0 errors and one warning: 1016, the dummy entity is not in the application model. That warning is expected for non-database entities.

Result

Ten forms, 310 fields, all generated from layout lists and the ProcScript source files. When a form needed a change - a label, a new button, a bug fix in the script - the source file changed, the XML was generated again and imported over the old form. After every import, the script in the repository was compared with the source file; all of them were identical.

The XML route does not replace the painter for a form that needs careful visual design. For many similar forms with a fixed pattern, it turned a lot of clicking into a list per form, and it made the layout reviewable as text.

title: How I handle ~1M requests a day on 1 vCPU and 2GB RAM (and keep bots out without user accounts)
summary:
I run a Tempgbox : free temporary email service on one vCPU and 2GB of RAM. Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery. It serves around a 1 million+ requests a day. Still i notice that backend use only 500 Mb ram and 1.5 GB ram free.

Four changes made the biggest difference for such a small server.

Cloudflare in front. I put Cloudflare in front of everything as a proxy. Most requests are for frontend pages, and Cloudflare caches those, so they never reach my server. That alone took a lot of load off it.

DRF to Django Ninja. I migrated the API from Django REST Framework to Django Ninja, which has built-in async support. I’m still learning how much that gives me, but it was the right direction for an API that does a lot of waiting.

Cleaning up guest users. Most of my users are guests, so guest accounts pile up fast. Now I delete a guest user as soon as their token expires. The database stays small, and I stopped paying to store people who were gone anyway.

Redis, with regular cleanup. I use Redis for short-lived data, and I clean it up on a schedule instead of letting it grow. With only 2GB of RAM, Redis can quietly eat memory that the rest of the stack needs, so I treat it like a cache that must stay small, not a place to dump things.

I’m curious what other people with tiny servers did first. Caching, cleanup, or something else?

title: Validate a CSV's shape before turning rows into dictionaries
summary:
A CSV import can succeed syntactically while still losing information. One small example is a repeated column name: two cells may be mapped to the same dictionary key. A row with too few fields can also become a dictionary with missing values instead of raising the error your application expected.

Before an import updates anything, it helps to define the shape of the input: which headers are acceptable, whether they must be unique, and how many fields each record must contain. This tutorial builds a small reader with an explicit contract rather than relying on a successful parse as proof of a valid file.

Define the contract first

The example below accepts UTF-8 files, with or without a byte-order mark, using the standard comma-separated dialect. It trims whitespace from header names only, rejects empty or duplicate names after trimming, and requires every nonblank record to match the header width.

Completely blank rows are skipped. An empty file is rejected, while a file containing only a valid header produces an empty list. Values remain strings, and spaces inside values are preserved.

Those choices are not universal CSV rules. They are the contract for this particular importer. If spaces distinguish two column names in your format, remove the header normalization and document that choice.

Read sequences before building dictionaries

Save this as checked_csv.py. It uses only the Python standard library.

import csv
from pathlib import Path


def read_checked_csv(path):
    with Path(path).open(encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as stream:
        reader = csv.reader(stream, strict=True)
        raw_headers = next(reader, None)
        if raw_headers is None:
            raise ValueError("CSV file is empty")
        headers = [name.strip() for name in raw_headers]
        if not headers or any(not name for name in headers):
            raise ValueError("Every column needs a non-empty header")
        if len(set(headers)) != len(headers):
            raise ValueError("Headers must be unique after trimming")
        records = []
        for row in reader:
            if not row:
                continue
            if len(row) != len(headers):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Record ending at line {reader.line_num}: "
                    f"expected {len(headers)} fields, got {len(row)}"
                )
            records.append(dict(zip(headers, row)))
        return records

The order matters. The program checks the header before creating any dictionaries, then checks each record's width before calling zip. A shorter or longer row therefore cannot silently pass through the dictionary-construction step.

The Python CSV documentation recommends opening CSV files with newline="". That lets the CSV reader handle line endings, including newlines inside quoted fields. The utf-8-sig decoder also handles an optional UTF-8 byte-order mark; see the codec documentation.

Try a quoted value

Create a file called sample.csv:

name,note
Mira,"tea, mint"
Noah,second item

Then run:

from checked_csv import read_checked_csv

print(read_checked_csv("sample.csv"))

The result is:

[{'name': 'Mira', 'note': 'tea, mint'}, {'name': 'Noah', 'note': 'second item'}]

The comma inside the quotation marks belongs to the value. Splitting each line with str.split(",") would not preserve that distinction. Using a CSV reader avoids implementing quoting behavior by hand.

Now replace the second record with Noah. The reader raises a ValueError explaining that the record has one field instead of two. Add an extra cell instead, and it reports the opposite mismatch.

The reported position is the physical line where the record ends, not a logical record number. That difference matters when a quoted value spans multiple lines. Do not label it a row index in an interface without explaining the distinction.

Test boundaries, not just the happy path

The function was executed with Python 3.11.3 against ten local fixtures:

Input condition Checked result
UTF-8 BOM, CRLF, quoted comma, multiline value, blank line Two records; quoted text preserved
Valid header with no records Empty list
Padded headers and padded values Header names trimmed; value spaces preserved
Repeated header Rejected
Duplicate created by trimming headers Rejected
Empty header name Rejected
Missing field Rejected
Extra field Rejected
Empty file Rejected
Unclosed quoted field Rejected by the CSV parser

All ten checks passed. The combined first fixture is important: several common formatting details can appear in one file, not only in isolated test cases.

For your own importer, add a fixture for the exact dialect you expect. Do not assume that a comma-separated example demonstrates support for semicolon-delimited exports. If the delimiter is configurable, test that configuration explicitly.

Keep structural checks separate from data validation

This function does not establish that the required columns exist. A file with headers animal,color is structurally acceptable even if your application expects name,note. Check the expected schema separately, after loading and before making changes.

It also does not validate dates, reject duplicate identifiers across records, convert numbers, detect every malformed CSV convention, or make cell values safe for a spreadsheet or HTML output. Those are separate requirements. strict=True improves parser error reporting; it does not turn the module into a complete schema validator.

The function collects every record in memory. That makes this small example convenient and means it returns only after the whole file passes its structural checks. Large imports may need a streaming design, explicit size limits, and a transaction or staging step to prevent partial updates.

Keep that boundary visible: a readable file, a structurally valid table, and data ready to commit are three different states. Handling them separately gives the importer useful failure points instead of one optimistic success message.

title: x402 Protocol: Machine-Native Micro-Settlements for AI Agents
summary:
x402 Protocol: Machine-Native Micro-Settlements for AI Agents

Agen AI mandiri tidak bisa membuka rekening bank. Mereka tidak memiliki kartu identitas untuk KYC Stripe, dan memberikan kartu kredit korporat ke loop eksekusi LLM yang tidak deterministik adalah resep bencana likuiditas.

Ketika software mulai membeli compute, data, atau context window dari software lain, infrastruktur pembayaran fiat kita yang berbasis batch 30 hari langsung patah. Web membutuhkan primitif moneter yang dirancang untuk mesin: granularitas sub-sen, latensi sub-detik, dan verifikasi deterministik langsung pada lapisan protokol transfer data.

Solusinya bukan API gateway terpusat baru. Solusinya adalah menghidupkan kembali kode status HTTP yang telah lama diabaikan: 402 Payment Required.

Masalah: API Gateway Tradisional Membunuh Otonomi Agen

Arsitektur saat ini memaksa agen beroperasi dalam batas-batas manusia:

  1. Pendaftaran manual via OAuth/Email.
  2. Konfigurasi kartu kredit dengan batasan penagihan bulanan minimum ($5 - $10).
  3. Penerbitan API key statis yang rentan bocor.

Jika Agen A ingin membeli 500 token inferensi Llama-3 dari Agen B, biaya riilnya mungkin $0.0004. Sistem pembayaran kartu mengenakan biaya tetap $0.30 + 2.9% per transaksi. Unit economics-nya langsung runtuh.

x402 membalik paradigma ini: jangan gunakan akun. Gunakan transaksi kriptografis per-request.

Arsitektur Alur x402

Protokol x402 menyatukan handshake HTTP standar dengan verifikasi kriptografi terdesentralisasi:

  1. Request: Klien (agen AI) mengirim request HTTP GET/POST biasa ke resource endpoint.
  2. Challenge: Server merespons dengan HTTP 402 Payment Required, menyertakan payload header berisi:
    • Alamat penerima pembayaran (Base L2).
    • Biaya per-panggilan dalam format satuan terkecil (misalnya Wei atau USDC base units).
    • Nonce unik atau hash tantangan kriptografis untuk mencegah replay attack.
  3. Settlement: Agen klien menandatangani transaksi on-chain atau State Channel ticket, lalu mengulang request dengan menyertakan bukti bayar pada header X-Payment-Signature atau X-Payment-TxHash.
  4. Fulfillment: Server memverifikasi bukti di Base L2 secara instan via local node RPC cache, lalu mengalirkan respons. 
Client Agent                     Provider Node
     |                                 |
     |---- GET /v1/context ----------->|
     |<--- 402 Payment Required -------| (Headers: recipient, fee, nonce)
     |     [Sign & Broadcast L2 Tx]    |
     |---- GET + Header: X-Payment --->|
     |<--- 200 OK (Data Stream) -------|

Implementasi Lapangan: Base L2 Runtime

Base (Chain ID 8453) menjadi fondasi ideal untuk x402 karena biaya eksekusi transaksi yang konsisten di bawah $0.005 pasca-EIP-4844, serta ekosistem likuiditas USDC yang dalam.

Berikut implementasi klien Python otonom minimal yang menangani challenge 402 dan melakukan settlement langsung ke dompet kas penyedia jasa:

import os
import requests
from web3 import Web3
from eth_account import Account

# Base Mainnet RPC
RPC_URL = "https://mainnet.base.org"
w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(RPC_URL))

# Inisialisasi signer agen otonom
AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY = os.getenv("AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY")
agent_account = Account.from_key(AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY)

TARGET_ENDPOINT = "https://agent-node.internal/v1/inference"

def execute_autonomous_call():
    session = requests.Session()

    # 1. Probe endpoint
    resp = session.post(TARGET_ENDPOINT, json={"prompt": "Summarize block 120401"})

    if resp.status_code == 402:
        # Ekstraksi parameter penagihan
        recipient = resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Recipient", "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919")
        fee_wei = int(resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Amount-Wei", "10000000000000")) # 0.00001 ETH
        nonce_token = resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Nonce")

        # 2. Susun dan tanda tangani transaksi native settlement di Base (Chain ID 8453)
        tx = {
            'chainId': 8453,
            'nonce': w3.eth.get_transaction_count(agent_account.address),
            'to': recipient,
            'value': fee_wei,
            'gas': 21000,
            'maxFeePerGas': w3.to_wei('0.1', 'gwei'),
            'maxPriorityFeePerGas': w3.to_wei('0.01', 'gwei'),
            'data': w3.to_hex(text=nonce_token)  # Mengunci nonce challenge ke calldata
        }

        signed_tx = agent_account.sign_transaction(tx)
        tx_hash = w3.eth.send_raw_transaction(signed_tx.rawTransaction)

        # 3. Request ulang dengan bukti settlement terikat
        headers = {
            "X-Payment-TxHash": tx_hash.hex(),
            "X-Payment-Sender": agent_account.address
        }

        final_resp = session.post(
            TARGET_ENDPOINT, 
            json={"prompt": "Summarize block 120401"},
            headers=headers
        )
        return final_resp.json()

    return resp.json()

Validasi dan Mekanika Penampungan Kas

Di sisi penyedia, verifikasi transaksi tidak membutuhkan konfirmasi blok penuh jika menggunakan pre-confirmation atau probabilistic security untuk inferensi murah. Kas masuk dikonsolidasikan langsung ke treasury pool `0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd

title: Your Classifier Scored Ninety Six Percent Because the Same Emails Were in Both Halves
summary:
We trained a small model
to route support emails.

Delivery.

Billing.

Damaged goods.

Account changes.

Forty thousand labelled emails.

Shuffle them.

Eighty percent to train,
twenty percent to test.

The test score was ninety six percent.

We celebrated.

We shipped it.

In the first month
it routed about three in four correctly.

Same model.

Same kind of emails.

The test set was not lying.

It was answering
a different question
from the one we asked.

Here is what we found
when we finally read the data.

Our biggest customers
send the same email
over and over.

Their systems use templates.

Only the order number changes.

Some threads
had been labelled twenty times,
once per reply,
each one quoting the last.

A random split
puts copies of the same email
on both sides.

So the test was full
of emails the model had already seen
in training,
with a different number in them.

It did not have to understand
damaged goods.

It only had to remember
this customer's wording.

That is leakage.

Information from the test
reached the training,
and the score measured memory.

Production has no copies.

Next month's emails
are new.

The fix is to split
the way the future arrives.

Group by customer,
or by thread,
so everything from one source
lands on one side.

In scikit-learn
that is GroupShuffleSplit,
or GroupKFold for cross validation.

Remove near duplicates
before you split,
not after.

And when the data has dates,
train on the past
and test on the most recent weeks.

Our honest score
came out at seventy nine.

Lower,
and true.

It matched production
within a point or two,
and for the first time
we knew which number to improve.

This does not only apply
to models you train.

If you test a prompt
on examples you also put in the prompt,
or tune it on the cases
you then grade it on,
the same thing happens.

Before you trust a score,
ask what the test had
that tomorrow will not.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: You Unpacked the Customer's Archive With tarfile and One File Landed Outside the Folder
summary:
Customers sent us their photos
as one archive.

A tar.gz,
because their system made one.

The service did the obvious thing.

with tarfile.open(path) as tar:
tar.extractall(upload_dir)

A temporary folder per upload.

Read the images.

Delete the folder.

Tidy.

Then someone sent an archive
with a member called

../../app/templates/base.html

Python did
exactly what the archive said.

It joined the folder
and the name,
walked up two levels,
and wrote the file there.

Over ours.

An archive is not a bag of files.

It is a list of instructions.

Put this content
at this path.

Make this a link
to that location.

Give it these permissions.

Every one of those
was written by the sender.

The same mistake
has been made in every language.

A loop over zip entries
in Java,
new File(target, entry.getName()),
no check.

In 2018
it was common enough
to get a name.

Zip Slip.

The tarfile weakness
was reported against Python
in 2007,
and for years
the documentation
carried a warning
instead of a fix.

Python 3.12 added a filter argument.

tar.extractall(upload_dir, filter="data")

It refuses absolute paths,
refuses names that climb out,
refuses links that point outside,
and strips the dangerous permission bits.

From 3.14
that filter is the default.

Until every server you run
is on 3.14,
write it yourself.

Being explicit costs one argument,
and the code then means the same thing
on every version.

On any other language,
check every entry before you write it.

Resolve the full destination.

Confirm it still sits
inside the folder you chose.

Skip links entirely
unless you truly need them.

Treat the names
like any other user input.

Because they are.

Then make the blast smaller.

Unpack in a directory
the process can write to
and nothing else.

Not as the user
that owns your code.

And limit the total size
and the number of members
before you start.

Whenever your code
obeys a file
it did not write,
someone else is writing your code.

– Serguey Asael Shinder
